title: North and West Africa
hook: the Maliki school is followed from Morocco to Nigeria, often praying with hands at the sides

segments.voice: Yesterday, the practice of Medina, and your line: the living practice. What did you see a community do without explaining it, and did anyone tell you why? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

A row of worshipers stands shoulder to shoulder in a mosque in Fez, or Dakar, or Kano. The imam says Allahu akbar and the prayer begins. Look along the row at their hands. Some are folded over the chest or the stomach. Others hang straight down, loose at the sides, the whole way through the standing. A visitor from Istanbul or Lahore might wonder if something was forgotten. Nothing was. Those loose hands are one of the quiet signatures of the school we've followed these last few days, carried a long way from Malik's Medina. Today: North and West Africa.
screen: `A ROW OF WORSHIPERS IN FEZ.` → `SOME HANDS FOLDED, SOME AT THE SIDES.` → `NOTHING WAS FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: First, the map. The Maliki school traveled west from Medina, along the North African coast and down across the Sahara. Today it's followed across Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya, in Mauritania, and down through West Africa, in Senegal, Mali and northern Nigeria, among other places. Scholars carried it: teachers in Kairouan in Tunisia, students in Spain, and later the scholars of Timbuktu, with their manuscript libraries. Next, the hands. The posture has a name, sadl, letting the arms hang. In the Mudawwana, an early Maliki book recording Malik's answers, he's reported to have disliked folding the hands in the obligatory prayer. Maliki scholars give reasons: that it was the practice they received in Medina, and that it guards against leaning or showing off. Then, the honest complication. Malik's own Muwatta records a report that people were told to place the right hand over the left in prayer. So the question was never simple, even inside the school. Some Malikis fold their hands, and they too point to Malik. Both postures are found in Maliki mosques, sometimes in the same row. Last, why it matters. A visitor who sees hands at the sides is seeing the practice of Medina, as one school received it, still standing in a mosque in West Africa. The other Sunni schools fold their hands, in slightly different places, and Shia Muslims pray with their arms at their sides too. Each can tell you why. And the prayer behind the imam is one prayer, whatever the hands are doing.
screen: `WEST FROM MEDINA, ACROSS THE SAHARA.` · `SADL: THE ARMS HANG.` · `THE MUWATTA RECORDS FOLDING TOO.` · `ONE PRAYER, WHATEVER THE HANDS DO.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice another way of standing. If you can stand, stand. If not, sit tall. Let your arms hang loose at your sides. Feel the weight in your fingers, the slight pull on your shoulders. Breathe. Now, slowly, fold your hands in front of you and feel how different that is: closed, gathered. Then let them fall again. Each is a way someone received. Stay with your hands at your sides for the rest of the time. If you pray, you can remember Muslims standing this way in a row somewhere right now. The bell holds the time.
North and West Africa. Where the Maliki school is followed, from Morocco to Nigeria, often with hands held at the sides in prayer. Today's word.
Your line: hands at the sides. Today, when you see someone do a familiar thing in an unfamiliar way, ask where they received it before you decide it's wrong. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.
